entities.name: Georg von Speyer
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Georg von Speyer, born Georg Hohermuth, was a pivotal German conquistador and governor who spearheaded early European exploration and exploitation of Venezuela's interior from 1534 until his death in 1540. Appointed governor of Klein-Venedig (Little Venice), the vast territory granted by Charles I of Spain to the Welser banking family of Augsburg, Speyer's tenure marked a significant, albeit brutal, chapter in the German involvement in the Spanish colonization of the Americas. He is often recognized by his Spanish name, Jorge de Espira, reflecting the cultural synthesis of his expeditions.

Upon his arrival in Coro in 1534, Speyer, alongside Nikolaus Federmann and Philipp von Hutten, embarked on extensive and arduous expeditions deep into the Venezuelan Llanos and foothills of the Andes, driven by the persistent allure of El Dorado and other rumored gold-rich lands. His most significant undertaking was a three-year journey (1535–1538) across the plains, reaching as far as the Caguán River in present-day Colombia, facing relentless resistance from various indigenous groups like the Caquetío and Jirajara, and enduring immense logistical challenges and loss of life among his European and indigenous contingents. These expeditions, while failing to locate El Dorado, provided the first detailed European reconnaissance of vast swathes of the South American continent.
